His utterance is sought in the congregation, he smiles quietly, stands outside a house he has not been invited into, and is grieved at disgrace. His words are weighed in the balance, and his mouth is his heart. Instruction is to him an ornament of gold.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 21
s: Wisdom is described as the fulfilment of the fear of the Lord, and grace is found on the lips of the wise. To a fool it is like a house that is destroyed.

l: sinners, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 21
s: The way of sinners is paved with stones, and at its end is the pit of Hades. One who hates reproof is on the path of the sinner, and the congregation of wicked men is like a bundle of tow with a flame at its end.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 22
s: Chapter 22 uses comparisons to describe the slothful man, the undisciplined or shameful child, and especially the fool. The slothful man is likened to a defiled stone and a dunghill, and a foolish or arrogant daughter brings shame on her father and husband. Teaching a fool is compared to gluing potsherds or waking a sleeper, and the fool is said to be heavier than lead, sand, salt, or iron, deserving lifelong mourning and avoidance. The chapter contrasts a heart settled on wise counsel, which stands firm, with the fearful heart of a fool. It ends by discussing friendship: insulting a friend dissolves the bond, but reconciliation is possible except after insult, arrogance, secret disclosure, or a treacherous blow, and the speaker pledges loyalty to a friend and asks for a guard on his own mouth.

l: slothful man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 22
s: The slothful man is compared to a defiled stone and to the filth of a dunghill. Everyone hisses at him in his disgrace, and anyone who picks him up shakes him off their hand.

l: fool, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 22
s: The fool is described as one who is hard to teach, like glued potsherds or a man roused from deep sleep, and as heavier than lead, sand, salt, or iron. Mourning for him lasts all the days of his life, and the reader is told not to talk much with him, to beware of him, and to turn away to find rest. His fearful heart, shaped by his own imagination, cannot stand against any fear, like fences on a high place in the wind.

l: friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 22
s: A friend may be wronged by a drawn sword or an opened mouth without the relationship being lost. He will flee, however, from insult, arrogance, disclosure of a secret, or a treacherous blow. The speaker declares he will not be ashamed to shelter a friend or hide from his face, though he warns that if evil comes to him through the friend, those who hear of it will beware of him.

l: friendship and reconciliation, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 22
s: Friendship is dissolved by insults, as a stone cast at birds scares them away, and insults precede bloodshed as smoke precedes fire. Reconciliation remains possible after a sword drawn or words spoken against a friend, but not after insult, arrogance, disclosure of a secret, or a treacherous blow. Faithfulness to a neighbor in poverty and affliction is urged so that one may share his gladness and inheritance in prosperity.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: Chapter 23 opens with the speaker praying to the Lord, addressed as Father and Master of his life, not to be abandoned to the counsel of his adversaries and asking for discipline over his thoughts, haughty eyes, evil desire, gluttony, and lust. He then instructs his children in the discipline of the mouth, warning against habitual oaths, naming the Holy One, gross rudeness, and abusive language, which bring sin, calamity, and shame. The chapter condemns the fornicator and the adulterous man, who falsely believes darkness and walls hide him, though the Lord's eyes see all things, and he will be punished and seized unexpectedly. It likewise condemns the wife who leaves her husband and bears an heir by another man, citing three offenses, and says she will be brought before the congregation, her children will not take root, and her memory will be a curse. Those left behind learn that nothing is better than the fear of the Lord or sweeter than heeding his commandments.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: The Lord is addressed as Father and Master of the speaker's life and as Father and God of his life, and the speaker begs him not to abandon him to his adversaries' counsel. His eyes are described as ten thousand times brighter than the sun, seeing all human ways and secret places, and he knew all things before they were created and after they were completed.

l: speaker (author praying), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: The speaker prays that the Lord will not abandon him, asks for scourges over his thought and a discipline of wisdom over his heart, and asks that haughty eyes, evil desire, gluttony, lust, and a shameless mind be kept from him. He then addresses his children, urging them to learn the discipline of the mouth.

l: discipline of the mouth, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: The speaker teaches that whoever keeps the discipline of the mouth will not be caught, while the sinner, the insulter, and the arrogant stumble through their lips. It means avoiding habitual oaths, naming the Holy One, gross rudeness, and abusive language.

l: oaths, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: The text warns against accustoming the mouth to oaths or to continually uttering the Name, comparing the swearer to a continually scourged servant who never lacks bruises. A man of many oaths is filled with iniquity, the scourge does not leave his house, and if he swears falsely he is not justified and his house is filled with calamities.

l: fornicator, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: The fornicator is described as a hot passion like a burning fire that is not quenched until it is consumed. All bread is sweet to him, and he will not cease until he has burned out the fire and until he dies.

l: adulterous man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: The man who strays from his marriage bed tells himself that darkness and walls hide him and that the Most High will not remember his sins. He fears human eyes but does not know the Lord sees everything, and he will be punished in the city streets and seized where he least expects it.

l: adulterous wife, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: The wife who leaves her husband and produces an heir by another man is charged with three offenses: disobeying the law of the Most High, trespassing against her husband, and committing adultery and bearing children by another man. She will be brought out into the congregation, her punishment will extend to her children, who will not take root, and she will leave a memory that is a curse with a reproach that is not blotted out.

l: fear of the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 23
s: Those left behind after the punishment of the adulterous wife will learn that nothing is better than the fear of the Lord. They will also learn that nothing is sweeter than heeding the Lord's commandments.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 24
s: Chapter 24 is a speech in which Wisdom praises herself among the people and in the congregation of the Most High. She says she came from the mouth of the Most High, roamed heaven, the abyss, and every nation seeking rest, and was then commanded by the Creator to dwell in Jacob and Israel. She ministered in the tabernacle, was established in Zion, and had her domain in Jerusalem, where she grew like cedars, palms, olives, and fragrant spices. She invites those who desire her to eat and drink of her fruits, promising they will not be ashamed or sin. The text identifies all this with the book of the covenant and the law of Moses, compares her abundance to great rivers, and closes with Wisdom saying her stream has become a sea and that she labors for all who seek wisdom.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 24
s: Wisdom praises herself, saying she came from the mouth of the Most High, was created before the ages, and will never cease to exist. After seeking rest among all peoples, she was told to dwell in Jacob, ministered in the tabernacle, and took root in Zion and Jerusalem. She likens herself to trees and perfumes, invites all who desire her to be filled, and says her stream grew into a river and a sea and that she labors for all who seek wisdom.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 24
s: The Most High is the one from whose mouth Wisdom came, and in whose congregation she speaks. As Creator of all things, he created her from the beginning, gave her a command, and told her to dwell in Jacob with her inheritance in Israel. He is also described as the one who makes wisdom, understanding, and instruction abundant like great rivers.

l: Jacob, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 24
s: Jacob is where the Creator commanded Wisdom to make her dwelling. The assemblies of Jacob are also named as those for whom Moses commanded the law as an inheritance.

l: Israel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 24
s: Israel is named as the place of Wisdom's inheritance, according to the Creator's command to her.

l: Zion, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 24
s: Zion is where Wisdom was established after she ministered before the Most High in the holy tabernacle.

l: Jerusalem, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 24
s: Jerusalem is called the beloved city, where the Creator gave Wisdom rest. It is the place of her domain.

l: book of the covenant, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 24
s: The book of the covenant is identified with all that Wisdom has said, and is described as the book of the covenant of the Most High God. It is the law that Moses commanded for an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25
s: Chapter 25 is a wisdom sermon listing things the speaker finds beautiful, hateful, and happy. He enjoys harmony among kindred, neighbors, and spouses, and hates the arrogant poor man, the lying rich man, and the adulterous old fool. He praises the judgment, wisdom, and experience of the aged, and says the fear of the Lord surpasses everything, including wisdom. The second half turns to a long denunciation of the wicked woman, whom he calls worse than any wound or enemy, and who he says darkens her husband's life and began sin and death. He closes by advising a husband to deny such a woman freedom of speech and to cut her away if she does not obey.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25
s: The Lord is the one before whom harmony among kindred, neighbors, and spouses is beautiful. The one who fears him is called greater than anyone who has found wisdom.

l: wicked woman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25
s: She is described as the worst wickedness and malice, worse than any wound, calamity, or enemy's wrath, and the speaker would rather live with a lion and a dragon than with her. She changes her appearance and darkens her countenance like a bear, and is blamed as the beginning of sin and the cause of death. The speaker advises denying her freedom of speech and cutting her away from the husband's flesh if she does not go as directed.

l: husband (of the wicked woman), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25
s: He is described as sitting among his neighbors and sighing bitterly when he hears of his wife's conduct. Living with a talkative wife is likened to climbing a sandy hill for aged feet, and a wife who will not make him happy leaves him with hanging hands and weak knees, a saddened countenance, and a wounded heart. He is advised not to be ensnared by a woman's beauty and to cut off a wife who will not follow his direction.

l: fear of the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25
s: The fear of the Lord is called the glory of the aged and said to surpass all things. No one is greater than the one who fears the Lord, and the question is asked to whom its holder could be compared.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25
s: Wisdom is called beautiful in old men, and the one who finds it is called great. Yet no one is greater than the one who fears the Lord.

l: elderly people, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25
s: The aged are praised for beautiful judgment, knowledge of good counsel, and wisdom, with much experience as their crown and the fear of the Lord as their glory. Those who gathered nothing in youth are warned they will find nothing in old age, and an old fool who is an adulterer is hated. Walking up a sandy hill is used as an image of what a wife full of words is to a quiet man, compared with its effect on aged feet.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 26
s: Chapter 26 praises the good wife and warns about the wicked or unrestrained woman. A good wife brings her husband joy, peace, doubled days, and delight, and her beauty, modesty, and self-control are compared to the sun, a lampstand, and golden pillars on silver. The speaker names three things his heart fears: slander of a city, a mob assembly, and false accusation, all worse than death. Women who are jealous, drunken, or sexually unfaithful are condemned, and a headstrong daughter is to be watched closely. The text also lists grievous sights, including a warrior in poverty, wise men treated as garbage, and one who turns from righteousness to sin, and notes that merchants and retailers struggle to avoid sin.

l: good wife, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 26
s: A good wife is called a great gift given to those who fear the Lord. She gives her husband joy and peace, delights him with her grace, and strengthens him with her knowledge. Her silence, modesty, and self-control are valued above measure, and her beauty in a well-organized home is likened to the sun rising, a lamp on the holy lampstand, and golden pillars on a silver base.

l: husband, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 26
s: The husband of a good wife is called happy, and the number of his days will be doubled. He fulfills his years in peace, is delighted by her grace, and has his bones strengthened by her knowledge. By contrast, the man who takes hold of a wicked woman is compared to one grasping a scorpion.

l: wicked woman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 26
s: A wicked woman is likened to a chafing yoke, and whoever takes hold of her is like one who grasps a scorpion. The text also condemns the jealous woman whose tongue-lashing is known to all, the drunken woman who causes great wrath and does not cover her shame, and the woman whose fornication shows in her raised eyes and eyelids. She is described as opening her mouth like a thirsty traveller and drinking from every nearby water.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: Chapter 27 warns that profit-seeking invites sin and that a household without the fear of the Lord is quickly overthrown. It teaches that a person's thoughts and speech reveal his character, comparing them to a sieve, a furnace testing a potter's vessels, and a tree's fruit. It contrasts the wise discourse of the godly with the offensive, swearing, quarrelsome talk of fools and the proud. It strongly condemns the one who reveals a friend's secrets, since trust and friendship are lost and cannot be recovered. It closes by describing the deceitful schemer and evildoers, whose harm rebounds on them, and says the Lord hates the schemer and that wrath and anger belong to the sinner.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: The Lord is the object of the fear that keeps a person's house from being quickly overthrown. The speaker says the Lord will hate the deceitful schemer.

l: sin, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: Sin is said to thrust itself in between buying and selling like a nail between stones, and to lie in wait for evildoers as a lion lies in wait for prey. Many have sinned for profit, and wrath and anger are called abominations that a sinner will possess.

l: thoughts, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: A person's thoughts are the test of the person, likened to a sieve that leaves refuse behind and a furnace that tests a potter's vessels. The utterance of the heart's thought discloses a person as fruit discloses a tree's cultivation, so no one should be praised before his thoughts are heard.

l: fools, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: Fools change like the moon, while the godly man's discourse is always wise. Their talk is offensive, their laughter wantonly sinful, and their swearing and strife make hair stand on end and others plug their ears; the reader is told to limit time among them.

l: one who reveals secrets, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: He destroys trust and will not find a close friend. He is compared to someone who lets a bird go or who lets a gazelle escape the snare, and he is without hope, unlike a wound or abuse that can be mended.

l: friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: The reader is told to love a friend and keep faith with him. A friend whose secrets are revealed goes far away and cannot be caught again, so the friendship is destroyed as an enemy is destroyed.

l: deceitful schemer, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: He winks the eye and contrives evil, and those who know him keep their distance. He speaks sweetly and admires your words when present, but afterward twists his speech and sets a trap in your words; the speaker hates him and says the Lord will hate him.

l: evildoers, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 27
s: Evildoers are told that their deeds will roll back upon them without their knowing where they came from. Like one who casts a stone upward, digs a pit, or sets a snare, they fall into their own traps, and sin lies in wait for them like a lion.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: Chapter 28 teaches that those who take vengeance will meet vengeance from the Lord, while those who forgive their neighbor's hurt will have their own sins pardoned when they pray. It urges the reader to remember death, the commandments, and the covenant of the Highest in order to stop enmity and anger. It warns that passionate and sinful men kindle strife and discord, comparing quarrels to a fire that spreads according to its fuel, and to a spark that can be blown or quenched by the same mouth. It then condemns the whisperer and slanderer, whose tongue destroys peace, scatters peoples, topples cities, and breaks bones more deadly than the sword, with a yoke of iron and bands of brass. It closes by advising the reader to guard words with a balance, a door, and a bar, as one guards silver and gold with thorns, lest he slip and fall.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: The Lord is said to bring vengeance upon the one who takes vengeance and to make his sins firm. He is the one from whom healing is sought, and those who forsake him fall into the slanderous tongue's fire, while godly men are not ruled or burned by it.

l: vengeance, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: Vengeance is presented as self-defeating: whoever takes it will find vengeance from the Lord, and his sins will be made firm.

l: anger and wrath, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: Anger and wrath are described as nourished by a man who is himself flesh, leaving no one to atone for his sins. The reader is told to stop enmity and not be angry with his neighbor, and a man's wrath is said to match his strength and wealth, like a fire matching its fuel.

l: forgiveness, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: Forgiving a neighbor the hurt he has done is the condition for having one's own sins pardoned when praying. The text asks how anyone can harbor anger and still expect healing from the Lord.

l: neighbor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: The neighbor is the person who may have done hurt and who should be forgiven. The reader is told not to be angry with him and to overlook ignorance.

l: vengeful man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: The vengeful man harbors anger, has no mercy on a man like himself, and cannot rightly make supplication for his own sins. He will find vengeance from the Lord, and his sins will be made firm.

l: strife, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: Strife is something to abstain from, since doing so diminishes one's sins, and a passionate man kindles it. A contention begun in haste kindles a fire, and hasty fighting sheds blood, with the fire burning as its fuel allows.

l: whisperer, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: The whisperer, called double-tongued, is to be cursed because he has destroyed many who were at peace. As a slanderer he has shaken many, dispersed them from nation to nation, pulled down strong cities, overthrown great men's houses, and cast out brave women and deprived them of their labors.

l: tongue, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 28
s: The tongue is likened to a spark that burns when blown on and is quenched when spat upon, both coming from the mouth. Its stroke breaks bones, it has felled more people than the sword, and its yoke is iron and its bands brass. The reader is told to put a balance, weight, door, and bar on his mouth to guard his words.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: Chapter 29 instructs readers on lending, almsgiving, and suretyship, and warns about dependent living. It urges merciful people to lend to a neighbor in need and to repay on time, while describing borrowers who flatter before receiving a loan and then make excuses, repay half, or curse their creditor. It tells readers to be patient with a poor man, to give alms for the commandment's sake, and to store up almsgiving as protection greater than a shield or spear. It praises the guarantor who stands surety for a neighbor, condemns the thankless sinner who ruins him, and warns that suretyship has ruined prosperous people and driven them abroad. It ends by naming life's essentials, preferring a modest home to sumptuous fare in another man's house, and depicting the humiliation of a sojourner who is made to serve a host and then ordered out.

l: neighbor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: The neighbor is the one to whom a merciful person lends in time of need, and the lender is told to repay him on time and keep faith with him. He is also the person for whom a good man will be surety, and the reader is told to help him according to his power while taking care not to fall himself.

l: borrower (the one who receives a loan), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: Many borrowers treat a loan as a windfall, kissing the lender's hands and speaking submissively until they receive the money. When payment is due they delay, make excuses, and blame the season, and they may repay only half or pay with cursing, railing, and disgrace instead of honor, making an enemy of the creditor without cause.

l: creditor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: The creditor who lends to a neighbor in need is acting mercifully and keeping the commandments. If the borrower prevails, the creditor will hardly receive half, and otherwise he loses his money and gains an enemy, so that many have turned away from lending out of fear of being defrauded. The insults of creditors are named among the things grievous to a man of understanding.

l: loan, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: A loan is to be given to a neighbor in time of need and repaid on time. Many have treated loans as windfalls and caused trouble for those who helped them, and this fraud has led many to refuse to lend.

l: poor man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: The poor man is to be treated with patience and not kept waiting for alms, and he is not to be sent away empty according to his need. His life under a shelter of logs is called better than sumptuous fare in another man's house.

l: almsgiving, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: Almsgiving is commended as keeping the commandments of the Most High, and it is said to profit more than gold. Stored up in one's store-chambers, it will deliver from all affliction and fight against an enemy better than a mighty shield and a ponderous spear.

l: guarantor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: A good man will be surety for his neighbor, and the one helped is told not to forget the guarantor's kindness because he has given his life for him. A sinner will waste the guarantor's property, and the thankless person fails the one who delivered him.

l: suretyship, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: Being surety has undone many who were prospering, shaking them like a wave of the sea and driving mighty men from their homes to wander among foreign nations. A sinner who falls into suretyship and undertakes contracts for work will fall into lawsuits.

l: sojourner, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: The sojourner lives a miserable life going from house to house, and as a guest dares not open his mouth. He is told to set a table and feed his host from what he has, and is then ordered to leave because an honored guest, the host's brother, has arrived.

l: host, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: The host in this passage treats the sojourner harshly, ordering him to set the table and feed him from what is in his hand. He then dismisses the sojourner, saying that an honored guest has come and that he needs his house.

l: hospitality, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 29
s: Hospitality as depicted here is a burden for the dependent guest, who must entertain, serve drinks, and receive no thanks along with bitter words. The text prefers being content with little or much in one's own home, listing water, bread, a garment, and a house for privacy as life's essentials.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 30
s: Chapter 30 first urges a father to discipline his son strictly, promising that the father will gain joy, pride before friends, honor against enemies, and a legacy in a son like himself. It warns that pampering, playing with, or giving liberty to a child leads to fear, grief, stubbornness, and sorrow, comparing an unrestrained son to an unbroken horse. The chapter then turns to health, saying a healthy poor man is better than a sick rich one, and that health of body and joy of heart surpass gold and wealth. It says death is better than bitter life and compares good things given to the afflicted to offerings laid on a grave or before an idol. It closes by urging the reader not to give the soul to sorrow, since gladness and cheerfulness lengthen life while envy, wrath, and anxiety shorten it.

l: son, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 30
s: The son is to be chastised, given work, and kept from liberty in youth, lest he become stubborn, headstrong, disobedient, and shameless. If well taught, he brings his father joy and, after the father's death, stands as one like him, an avenger against enemies and one who repays kindness to friends. An unrestrained son is likened to an unbroken horse.

l: father (the father of the son), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 30
s: The father who loves his son lays stripes on him and thereby gains joy, profit, boasting among acquaintances, and rejoicing before friends. He dies as though not dead because he leaves behind a son like himself, and he dies without regret. One who makes too much of his son will bind up the boy's wounds and be troubled at every cry, and one who pampers or plays with him will be made afraid and grieved.

l: discipline and chastisement of children, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 30
s: The chapter commends strict discipline: laying stripes on a son, bowing down his neck, beating him on the sides in childhood, and giving him work. It says this brings profit, joy, and honor to the father, while pampering, laughing and playing with the child, and ignoring his follies lead to sorrow, gnashing of teeth, and a stubborn, disobedient child.

l: health, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 30
s: Health is said to be better than all gold and wealth without measure; a poor man who is healthy and fit is better off than a rich man afflicted in body. Death and eternal rest are said to be better than a bitter life and continual sickness. Good things given to one who cannot enjoy them are compared to food offerings on a grave or before an idol.

l: sorrow, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 30
s: The reader is told not to give his soul to sorrow or afflict himself deliberately. Sorrow is said to have destroyed many and to bring no profit, so it should be removed far away. Envy, wrath, and anxiety are likewise said to shorten life and bring old age before its time.

l: gladness and cheerfulness, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 30
s: Gladness of heart is called the life of a man, and cheerfulness lengthens his days. There is said to be no gladness above the joy of the heart. The reader is urged to love his own soul and comfort his heart, and the cheerful and merry are said to benefit from their food.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 31
s: Chapter 31 warns first against the sleeplessness and ruin that come from pursuing riches, noting that the rich man toils to gather money while the poor man toils in lack, and that many have been destroyed for gold. It praises the rich person who is found blameless and does not go after gold, whose prosperity will be made sure and whose alms the congregation will proclaim. The middle of the chapter instructs a guest at a great table to avoid greed, to consider his neighbor's feelings, to eat like a human being, to stop first, and to take moderate portions, since moderate eating brings healthy sleep while insatiable eating brings colic and wakefulness. It notes that people bless the man liberal with food and murmur against the stingy one. The chapter ends with advice on wine: do not show valor in it, drink it in season and moderation for joy, avoid excess that brings bitterness, rage and wounds, and do not rebuke or distress a neighbor at a wine banquet.

l: riches, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 31
s: Wakefulness from riches consumes the flesh, and anxiety about them takes away sleep. Love of gold is called a stumbling block that has given many over to ruin and that takes every fool, so the one who loves it will not be justified.

l: rich man (the rich person), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 31
s: The rich man toils in gathering money together and, when he rests, is filled with his good things. The rich person who is found blameless and does not go after gold is called blessed, having done wonderful things among his people; his prosperity will be made sure and the congregation will proclaim his alms.

l: greed at table, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 31
s: The guest at a great table is told not to be greedy or remark on how much food is there. A greedy eye is called a wicked thing, the most greedy thing created, which sheds tears from every face, and one should not stretch a hand wherever the eye looks or thrust it into the dish. The insatiable man suffers wakefulness, colic and griping, and risks being hated and offending.

l: table manners and moderate eating, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 31
s: The text counsels considering one's neighbor's feelings, being discreet, eating like a human being what is set before one, being first to stop for manners' sake, and not reaching out before others. A very little suffices the well-mannered man, and moderate eating brings healthy sleep, early rising and clear wits; one forced to eat should rise in the middle of it. People bless the one liberal with food, while the city murmurs against the stingy one.

l: wine, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 31
s: Wine has destroyed many, and it tests hearts in the quarreling of the proud as a furnace tests steel. Drunk in season and moderation it is as good as life, created to make men glad, joy of heart and gladness of soul. Drunk excessively it brings bitterness of soul, provocation, conflict, rage, diminished strength and wounds, and one should not rebuke or distress a neighbor at a wine banquet.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: Chapter 32 gives instruction on proper conduct at a feast and in life generally. A person made ruler of a feast should stay humble, serve the guests first, and then sit down to receive a wreath. Older speakers may talk but with sound knowledge and without interrupting the music, while a young man should speak only if obliged and asked, no more than twice, and briefly. Music at a wine banquet is compared to a ruby or emerald signet set in gold, and the reader is told to enjoy himself, avoid proud speech, and bless his Maker. The second half contrasts those who fear the Lord, who accept discipline and seek the law, with sinners and hypocrites who shun reproof, and urges counsel, caution, and guarding one's soul by keeping the commandments.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: The Lord is called the reader's Maker, who gives people to drink freely of his good things and should be blessed for them. Those who fear him receive discipline and find favor, and those who trust in him will suffer no loss.

l: feast ruler, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: The feast ruler is told not to be lifted up but to be among the guests as one of them. He should take care of them first and then sit down, and after finishing his duties he is gladdened on their account and receives a wreath for good service.
